summary: Registers seven mail transmission type keywords, ESMTPA, ESMTPS, ESMTPSA, LMTP, LMTPA, LMTPS and LMTPSA, for use in the with clause of a Received header. They show whether a message used extended SMTP or LMTP, with encryption or authentication.

plainLanguage.summary: These keywords let a Received header record whether a mail hop used ESMTP or LMTP and whether authentication or STARTTLS was negotiated. They are trace information, not proof that a connection was secure.

questions: what does esmtpsa mean in received header
subtitle: Seven keywords for recording ESMTP and LMTP transport details in Received headers.

tldr.problem: The Received header's with clause needed registered values for ESMTP or LMTP connections that used authentication or STARTTLS.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC registers ESMTPA, ESMTPS, ESMTPSA, LMTP, LMTPA, LMTPS, and LMTPSA as transmission types.
tldr.outcome: The keywords provide trace information but are not reliable security assurances and should not drive filtering decisions.

today: RFC 3848 is a Draft Standard. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Transmission Types Are Registered
sections.content:
The with clause in a message's Received header names the mail transmission protocol used for a hop. IANA maintains the registry of these protocol types; it already included SMTP and ESMTP.

This RFC adds keywords that distinguish ESMTP and LMTP, including cases where SMTP AUTH or STARTTLS was successfully negotiated.
sections.plainLanguage: A mail server records how a message arrived. These new values make that record more specific about the protocol and negotiated features.

sections.title: The Seven Keywords
sections.content:
ESMTPA means ESMTP with SMTP AUTH and successful authentication. ESMTPS means ESMTP with successfully negotiated STARTTLS. ESMTPSA indicates both. The corresponding LMTP values are LMTP, LMTPA, LMTPS, and LMTPSA.

The RFC reports that ESMTPA, ESMTPS, and ESMTPSA had been implemented in deployed server software for several years without reported problems.
sections.plainLanguage: The letters distinguish the transport and its negotiated features. A means authentication succeeded, S means STARTTLS was negotiated, and SA means both.

sections.title: Trace Information, Not Proof
sections.content:
The keywords provide informal trace information that can help diagnose email abuse after the fact. They do not reveal the details of the security mechanism used.

The values are not normally protected in transport and can be modified by an active attacker. The RFC says not to use them for filtering or relaying decisions except in very controlled environments; correlate Received headers with mail-transfer-agent logs for more reliable information.
sections.plainLanguage: The keywords can help investigate a message later, but an attacker may change them. They do not prove that a hop was secure.
